$comment: THE SCENARIO SCHEMA'S BUDGET HALF — GitHub issue #365, docs/38-what-the-game-is.md § 2.1, DECISIONS.md § D525 clause 1, and packages/viz/src/scenario/budget.ts for the shape and the argument. docs/38 § 2.1: "that record, plus a budget, is the scenario schema". Each stage below now carries a `budget`: what it opens with, and the ladder chimes can buy it up by. THERE IS DELIBERATELY NO GOAL, NO THRESHOLD, NO BAR AND NO DIFFICULTY ON A BUDGET — charter non-goal 6 and § D345 forbid buying a verdict, so two players who post the same run read the same verdict whatever they paid, and scenario/budget.ts REFUSES an unknown key on a budget rather than ignoring it, because a field that does not exist cannot be authored. The survivor count that makes a budget a difficulty is #367's and is NOT here: a count is a measurement and these are choices, so it is keyed by (scenarioId, stepId) in its own published table the way data/scenario-goals.json is keyed by stage id, and every step below carries the stable id it will be keyed by. PROVENANCE, per the product owner's 2026-09-08 standing ruling on governed data/ values: THESE FIGURES ARE AN AGENT'S PROPOSAL, drafted for the owner to accept, tighten or reject, and the line that ruling asks for is drawn field by field. What is DERIVED, from data/price-schedule.json and from each stage's own editable set, is the ARITHMETIC: a base is the dearest change the stage's own dials can reach plus the cheapest tier's typical (2 u); step 1 lifts the budget to the dearest equipment change (full-destination, 24 u); step 2 lifts it to the dearest change on the whole ladder (fifth-car, 54 u); and every schema ceiling is what the whole schedule costs (383 u — 368 until GitHub issue #431 added the 12 u regenerative-drive and 3 u counterweight-rebalance rows at the equipment tier, and 357 before GitHub issue #444 added the 11 u cabin-pressurisation row there; the ceiling is derived from data/price-schedule.json by packages/viz/src/scenario/budget.ts and moves whenever the ladder does, so this figure is a consequence of that file rather than a choice made here). What is CHOSEN is the RULE ITSELF — that a scenario opens one typical dispatcher change above its own dearest dial, and that the ladder has two rungs rather than one or four — and the chime price of each rung, set at one chime per unit bought because nothing measures an exchange rate and inventing a curve would be manufacturing precision. A price ladder is game feel, not a measurement, and no amount of arithmetic makes it one. So a reader disagreeing with a number here is disagreeing with a judgement, not correcting an error, and the lever is these fields rather than anything in code.

stages.name: One shaft, low demand
stages.teaches: a call, a car, a wait
brief: Garden Apartments is a small building with a gentle trickle of demand. Watch a call appear at a landing, a car answer it, and the wait end — those three things are what every dispatcher in this simulator is made of.

There is so little traffic here that most of the wait is decided before anyone presses a button: between calls the two cars simply sit wherever the last passenger left them, which is rarely where the next one is standing.
You can tell them where to wait instead, and the ground floor is only the first guess — try a few, and let the runs say which one this building actually wants.

stages.name: The morning rush
stages.teaches: rise and fall, and the gap between demand offered and demand carried
brief: Midtown Office at two and a half percent of its population arriving every five minutes: busy, and still under the level at which it stops coping.
Two counts matter here — how many people arrived, and how many were carried — and the gap between them is the thing a dispatcher can move.
This is the first stage where a number changes when you change a dial.

stages.name: Overwhelmed
stages.teaches: saturation, and why a diverging queue has no average
brief: The same building at the demand it actually ships with.
It cannot be won as configured, and that is the point: the queues grow faster than the cars empty them, so the tool refuses to average a wait that never settles.
Your job here is to read the refusal and say where the building broke, not to beat it.

stages.name: Two banks
stages.teaches: service zoning, and a journey with two waits
brief: Mixed-Use High-Rise has two banks that reach different parts of the building, so a single journey can involve two waits and a transfer.
Service zoning is which floors a shaft physically reaches — not who is allowed in, and not how the dispatcher thinks; the three are different concepts with different fixes.
Keep the queues from running away while you learn to tell them apart.

stages.name: Credentials
stages.teaches: access zoning, and the one problem no dial reaches
brief: Secure Tower puts a credential on most of its floors, and a few people every run are heading for one their badge does not open.

Those riders are turned away where they stand. It is not congestion and it is not the dispatcher: more cars would not carry them, and neither would a setting that reads the badge — a reader that can see the wrong badge still says no.
So watch what the rest of the run does. Everything you can move here is about the people who can travel, and the report counts the ones who could not beside the average rather than inside it.

stages.name: The tall one
stages.teaches: that at a hundred floors the geometry decides more than the weights do
brief: Vertical City is a hundred floors served by banks that each reach a slice of it, with sky lobbies where journeys change hands.
At this scale the shape of the building sets the outcome more than the weight vector does, and this stage is where that stops being an assertion.
Everything the other stages opened is open here. See how far the dials get you.

stages.teaches: that an improvement you cannot measure is not one
brief: Back to Midtown Office, at a level where both settings still stand behind their own numbers.

Every dimension the search space declares is yours to move, and the bar is no longer whether something looked better: it is a paired interval over fifty runs, on the difference itself, that does not contain zero.
Tune on the seeds you are given. The holdout set exists so that a gain living only in these passenger traces has somewhere to fail.

stages.name: The headline address
stages.teaches: that spare cars are not the same as a short interval
brief: Nineteen floors, 612 people, six cars at 5 m/s — the smallest crowd in the campaign on the tightest promise.
This is the only building here with more lift than it needs, and it still has to earn a 25 s interval. Capacity is not the constraint; where the spare cars wait between bursts is.
Watch the energy figure beside the wait. A car that drives more to be in the right place has spent something, and this is the stage where that trade is visible.

stages.name: Both ways at once
stages.teaches: demand with no dominant direction, and a car unlike its neighbours
brief: Guests arrive and leave all day, so there is no rush hour to point a dispatcher at — the traffic is two-way from the first minute to the last.

Four guest cars share the bank with one service lift at 1.75 m/s, less than two thirds their speed. Nothing in the configuration says it is the wrong car for a guest; only its speed and its capacity do.
A hard rule against reversing direction is worth less here than anywhere else in the campaign. It is on by default, and it is yours to turn off.

stages.name: The bed and the visitor
stages.teaches: that two cars in one bank can be the wrong car
brief: A hospital never empties, and its busiest moments are shift changes rather than a morning arrival.

Two of the five cars are bed lifts: bigger, slower, and the wrong answer to an ordinary hall call. They are in the same bank as the other three and the dispatcher has only their speed, capacity and transfer time to tell them apart.
Outpatients on floor 1 holds 180 people. When a clinic ends it empties downward — a crowd from the middle of the building rather than from the lobby, which is a shape no earlier stage produces.
